title.value: Kansas Billing Laws and Filing Deadlines We Track for You

paragraph.value: The insurers in Kansas have 30 days from the day they receive a clean claim to pay it or send a status notice, under K.S.A. 40-2442. In case of late payments, 1% interest per month is applied. After a request for records, the insurer has 15 days from receiving them to pay or deny. These are the rules for commercial payers. Medicare and Medicaid have their own rules.

title.value: 30-Day Prompt Payment Under K.S.A. 40-2442

paragraph.value: Under K.S.A. 40-2442, an insurer has 30 days from receipt to pay a clean claim or send notice of its status. The amounts which are not paid earn 1% interest per month. If the insurer asks for more information, you have 30 days to send it, and the insurer has 15 days after receiving it to pay or deny with specific reasons. The law covers state-regulated accident and sickness plans, not self-funded employer plans or Medicare.

title.value: 12-Month KanCare Fee-for-Service Filing Limit

paragraph.value: KMAP must receive a fee-for-service claim within 12 months of the date of service (K.S.A. 39-708a); inpatient claims are counted from the discharge date. From the date of service, the denied claim can be resubmitted after correction up to 24 months. However, a claim which is never submitted in the first 12 months cannot be recovered.

title.value: KanCare MCO Filing Windows

paragraph.value: Each KanCare MCO sets the filing window itself in its provider manual. This filing window is usually shorter than the fee-for-service limit. So, we track all the deadlines, not only one. On the payer’s side, K.S.A. 39-709f requires MCOs to process and pay clean claims within 30 days and all claims within 90 days, with 12% annual interest on late payments.

title.value: 18-Month Limit on Payer Recoupments

paragraph.value: There is a limit on recoupments in the same prompt payment statute. Under K.S.A. 40-2442, a commercial payer cannot recoup a payment which it says was made due to an error unless it begins within 18 months after the end of the month the payment was made. The only case that extends the window is fraud. We check the date on every refund request before a payment goes back.

title.value: Surprise Billing and the Federal No Surprises Act in Kansas

paragraph.value: Kansas has no broad state balance-billing law, so the federal No Surprises Act governs. Emergency care and out-of-network services provided at an in-network facility are billed to the patient at in-network cost sharing: copay, coinsurance, and deductible. Payment disputes between the provider and the plan go through the federal independent dispute resolution process. See the Kansas Insurance Department page on the No Surprises Act.

title.value: Telehealth Coverage Under the Kansas Telemedicine Act

paragraph.value: Under K.S.A. 40-2,213, in force since January 1, 2019, a Kansas plan cannot exclude a covered service only because it was delivered by telemedicine. The law does not require the plan to pay the in-person rate, so telehealth billing in Kansas means knowing each payer's telehealth fee schedule, modifiers and place-of-service rules.

title.value: How KanCare Medical Billing Works in Kansas

settings.description_text: Every provider starts with this and gets enrolled in the Kansas Medical Assistance Program. To get enrolled, providers use the KMAP provider portal operated by Gainwell Technologies, the state’s fiscal agent, and receive the KMAP provider ID. There is no KanCare MCO that will contract or pay without it, so this step unlocks everything that comes after it.

settings.title_text: Credential With Healthy Blue, Sunflower, and UnitedHealthcare
settings.description_text: KanCare 3.0 started from January 01, 2025 and it goes through December 31, 2027 with three plans: Healthy Blue, Sunflower Health Plan and UnitedHealthcare Community Plan. Aetna Better Health of Kansas left the program at the end of 2024. Each plan has a separate method of credentialing with its own forms, payer ID and portal.

settings.title_text: Verify MCO Assignment Before Every Visit
settings.description_text: Patients can change their plans, and the state can reassign them. A claim sent to the wrong MCO is denied even though the patient was covered. Our team checks assignments in the KMAP system before the visit and again before the claim is submitted. So, the plan on the claim is the plan on file for that date of service.

settings.title_text: Submit Claims Through KMAP or the MCO
settings.description_text: The claims under the fee-for-service umbrella go to the KMAP through their portal or EDI. Managed care claims go to the member’s MCO through its portal, EDI or clearinghouse. Paper KanCare claims are mailed to the MCO or its behavioral health or dental subcontractor, never to KMAP.

settings.title_text: Appeal Denials Within Each Plan's Window
settings.description_text: If there is a KanCare denial, the appeal goes to the MCO in the beginning and it should be inside the time window. If the plan upholds the denial, the next step is the state fair hearing. Missing the time window of the plan ends the appeal, so our denial management team logs each MCO’s deadline the day the remittance posts.

title.value: Where Revenue Slips With Each Kansas Payer
Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Kansas

paragraph.value: BCBSKS is headquartered in Topeka and covers 103 of Kansas’s 105 counties. The geography decides the route of the claims. A patient who is a resident of Johnson County carries a Blue KC card, not BCBSKS. We confirm the home plan before the claim is built.

title.value: Blue KC in Johnson and Wyandotte Counties

paragraph.value: Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Kansas City covers Johnson and Wyandotte counties plus the Missouri side of the metro. Even in the same city, it is a different payer ID and fee schedule. Claims sent to BCBSKS for a Blue KC member, or the other way round, lead to denials because the plan selected was wrong.

title.value: Medicare and Medicare Advantage in Kansas

paragraph.value: Kansas Part A and B claims are sent to WPS Government Health Administrators, the Jurisdiction 5 contractor. DME claims go to Noridian, home health and hospice claims are sent to CGS. Roughly a third of Kansas beneficiaries are in Medicare Advantage. There are 21 western counties that have no Medicare Advantage plan. Medicare Advantage plans have their own rules related to authorization and network. If the patient in the Medicare Advantage plan is treated like a patient in Original Medicare, this increases the risk of denials.

title.value: Marketplace Plans: Ambetter, UnitedHealthcare, Oscar, and Medica

paragraph.value: Kansas marketplace plans are sold through HealthCare.gov. For 2026 the issuers are Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Kansas, Ambetter from Sunflower Health Plan, UnitedHealthcare, Oscar, Medica and Blue KC, each in a different set of counties, and Medica leaves after 2026. Every plan is an EPO, so an out-of-network claim is denied rather than paid at a lower rate; we check network status before the visit.

title.value: Workers' Comp, SEHP, and TRICARE

paragraph.value: Workers' compensation claims are paid from the Kansas Department of Labor's Schedule of Medical Fees, at the lesser of the charge or the schedule. The State Employee Health Plan covers state workers and their families, concentrated around Topeka and Lawrence. They have their own carriers and plan rules. TRICARE West covers Fort Riley and Fort Leavenworth families, with their specific referral and authorization rules.

title.value: Rural Kansas Billing for Critical Access Hospitals, RHCs, and FQHCs

paragraph.value: There are 82 critical access hospitals in Kansas. 182 rural health clinics and 63 rural FQHC are there. Nearly 30% of Kansas live outside metro areas. (RHIhub; use the live counts). Rural billing is a different scenario when compared with physician billing. There are institutional claims, cost-based payments, payments based on encounter, and payer rules that are specifically for facilities.

settings.title_text: Critical Access Hospital Billing in Kansas

paragraph.value: Small rural hospitals get payments for the cost of their services. There is no specific price determined by anyone. The cost-based payment system of Medicare governs the critical access hospital billing insted of a fee schedule. Many Kansas critical access hospitals use swing beds, letting a patient move from hospital care to skilled nursing care in the same bed, and each part is billed separately under its own rules. Our hospital billing team manages CAH claims and the reconciliation behind them.

There is an all-inclusive rate per qualifying visit that is used for rural health clinic billing. The claim needs to show a billable counter with the right revenue code and qualifying visit line instead of fee-for-service CPT codes. Most of the rules that govern rural health clinics in Kansas are affiliated with the hospitals. This adds the provider-based rules. See our medical clinics billing service.

FQHCs bill Medicare a prospective payment per visit and KanCare is billed an encounter rate along with a wrap-around payment that reconciles to the PPS rate. The health centers in Kansas represented by the Community Care Network of Kansas, lose money when encounters are coded as visits that do not qualify. Our FQHC billing team manages these complexities.

title.value: A Medical Billing Company in Kansas That Fits Your Practice

paragraph.value: A medical billing company in Kansas has to fit the practice in front of it. A two-provider family practice in Salina, a behavioral health group billing all three MCOs, and a hospice billing CGS have little in common beyond the state line.

Home health and hospice: CGS claims, notices of election and face-to-face documentation.
Nursing homes: Part A SNF consolidated billing, KanCare nursing facility claims and the 12-month monthly filing rule.
Urgent care: S-codes where contracts allow, place of service 20 and same-day modifier 25.
Small practices: one biller's worth of work without one biller's single point of failure.
